subject: chemistry
pattern: Carries about 6-7 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: one or two 1-mark definitions (glycosidic linkage, peptide bond, essential amino acids, zwitterion), a 2-mark difference or reasoning (fibrous vs globular, denaturation, sucrose is non-reducing), a 3-mark question on DNA vs RNA, vitamins and their deficiency diseases or starch, and occasionally a 5-mark question on structure of glucose, protein structure levels or nucleic acids. Examiners expect textbook definitions in exact wording and neat comparison points.

questions.answer: The oxide linkage (-O-) formed between two monosaccharide units through oxygen atom by loss of a water molecule is called glycosidic linkage. Example: in sucrose, C1 of alpha-D-glucose is linked to C2 of beta-D-fructose by a glycosidic linkage.

questions.q: What are essential amino acids? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Amino acids which cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through diet are called essential amino acids. Examples: valine, leucine, isoleucine, lysine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, methionine, arginine, histidine (any two).

questions.q: What is a zwitterion? Why do amino acids behave like salts?
questions.answer: In aqueous solution the carboxyl group of an amino acid loses a proton and the amino group accepts it, giving a dipolar ion, H$_3$N$^+$-CHR-COO$^-$, called a zwitterion. Because of this ionic structure amino acids behave like salts: they have high melting points, are soluble in water and are amphoteric.

questions.q: Distinguish between fibrous proteins and globular proteins.
questions.answer: Fibrous proteins: polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds, forming fibre-like structures; they are insoluble in water; examples are keratin and myosin. Globular proteins: the chains coil around to give a spherical shape; they are soluble in water; examples are insulin and albumins.

questions.q: What is denaturation of protein? Give two examples.
questions.answer: When a protein in its native form is subjected to a physical change such as change of temperature, or a chemical change such as change of pH, the hydrogen bonds are disturbed; globules unfold and the helix gets uncoiled, so the protein loses its biological activity. This is called denaturation. The secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed but the primary structure remains intact. Examples: coagulation of egg white on boiling, curdling of milk.

questions.q: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar whereas maltose is a reducing sugar. Explain. What is invert sugar?
questions.answer: In sucrose, the reducing groups of both glucose (C1) and fructose (C2) are involved in the glycosidic bond, so there is no free aldehyde or ketone (hemiacetal) group; hence it does not reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent. In maltose, two alpha-D-glucose units are linked through C1-C4 and one glucose unit has a free hemiacetal (aldehydic) group at C1, so it is a reducing sugar. Invert sugar is the equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose obtained by hydrolysis of sucrose; it is laevorotatory.

questions.q: What are vitamins? Classify them with two examples each and mention one function of vitamin C.
questions.answer: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts in the diet for maintenance of growth and health; they are not synthesised in the body. They are classified by solubility. Fat soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K (stored in liver and adipose tissue). Water soluble vitamins: B group and C (excreted in urine and not stored, except B$_{12}$, so need regular supply). Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) prevents scurvy and helps in the formation of collagen.
keywords: fat soluble A, D, E, K

questions.q: Write any three differences between DNA and RNA.
questions.answer: DNA: (1) sugar is 2-deoxy-D-ribose; RNA: sugar is D-ribose. (2) DNA has bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine; RNA has adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil (uracil replaces thymine). (3) DNA has a double-stranded helical structure; RNA is single-stranded. (4) DNA is responsible for the transfer of hereditary characters (replication); RNA is responsible for protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA). (5) DNA is present mainly in the nucleus; RNA is mainly in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Mention the deficiency diseases caused by the lack of vitamins A, B$_1$, C, D and K.
questions.answer: Vitamin A (retinol): xerophthalmia (hardening of the cornea) and night blindness. Vitamin B$_1$ (thiamine): beri-beri (loss of appetite, nerve and muscle weakness). Vitamin C (ascorbic acid): scurvy (bleeding gums). Vitamin D: rickets in children (bone deformities) and osteomalacia in adults. Vitamin K: increased blood clotting time (haemorrhage). Also B$_{12}$: pernicious anaemia; vitamin E: increased fragility of red blood cells and muscular weakness.

questions.q: Describe the structure of starch. How does it differ from cellulose?
questions.answer: Starch is a polymer of alpha-D-glucose and has two components: amylose (15-20%), a water soluble, unbranched chain of glucose units linked by C1-C4 alpha-glycosidic bonds, and amylopectin (80-85%), water insoluble and branched with C1-C4 links in the chain and C1-C6 links at branch points. Cellulose is a straight chain polysaccharide of beta-D-glucose units joined by C1-C4 beta-glycosidic linkages. Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants and can be digested by humans; cellulose is the structural material of plant cell walls and cannot be digested by humans.

questions.q: Explain the formation of a peptide linkage. Name the types of bonds that stabilise the secondary and tertiary structure of proteins.
questions.answer: A peptide linkage (-CO-NH-) is the amide bond formed between the carboxyl group of one alpha-amino acid and the amino group of another with loss of a water molecule. NH$_2$CH$_2$COOH + NH$_2$CH(CH$_3$)COOH → NH$_2$CH$_2$CO-NHCH(CH$_3$)COOH + H$_2$O (glycylalanine, a dipeptide). Secondary structure (alpha-helix and beta-pleated sheet) is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups. Tertiary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges, ionic (salt) bridges and hydrophobic and van der Waals interactions.

questions.q: What are anomers? What are the evidences for the presence of the cyclic structure of glucose?
questions.answer: Anomers are two cyclic forms of a sugar that differ only in the configuration at C1 (the anomeric carbon): alpha-D-glucose (OH on C1 below the ring, m.p. 419 K, specific rotation +111°) and beta-D-glucose (OH above the ring, m.p. 423 K, +19.2°). Evidence for ring structure: (1) glucose does not give Schiff's test and 2,4-DNP/NaHSO$_3$ addition though it has an aldehyde group in open chain form. (2) The pentaacetate of glucose does not react with hydroxylamine, showing no free -CHO. (3) Glucose shows mutarotation, a change in optical rotation of the fresh solution to +52.5°, due to interconversion of the two anomers through the open chain form.

questions.q: Describe the structure of glucose: (i) any four evidences for the open chain structure with equations (ii) the cyclic (pyranose) structure.
questions.answer: Glucose is C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_6$, an aldohexose. Evidences: (1) Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane, so six carbons are in a straight chain. (2) It reacts with hydroxylamine to give oxime and with HCN to give cyanohydrin, showing a carbonyl group. (3) Oxidation with mild agent bromine water gives gluconic acid (six carbons), showing the carbonyl is an aldehyde. (4) With acetic anhydride it forms glucose pentaacetate, showing five -OH groups. (5) Oxidation with nitric acid gives saccharic acid, showing a primary alcohol group. Cyclic structure: the -OH on C5 adds to the C1 aldehyde group, forming a six-membered ring (pyranose, like pyran) with an extra asymmetric carbon C1, giving alpha and beta anomers, which explains why glucose does not give some aldehyde tests and shows mutarotation.

questions.q: Explain primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures of proteins.
questions.answer: Primary structure: the specific sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds in the polypeptide chain; any change in the sequence gives a different protein. Secondary structure: the shape in which a long polypeptide chain folds, stabilised by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups; two types: alpha-helix (right-handed coil, each N-H bonded to the C=O of the fourth residue, as in keratin) and beta-pleated sheet (chains side by side held by hydrogen bonds, as in silk). Tertiary structure: overall three-dimensional folding of the chain into fibrous or globular form, held by hydrogen bonds, disulphide bridges, ionic and hydrophobic interactions. Quaternary structure: spatial arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits with respect to each other, as in haemoglobin (four subunits).

questions.q: Describe the chemical composition of nucleic acids. Explain the double helix structure of DNA and mention the functions of DNA and RNA.
questions.answer: A nucleoside = sugar + nitrogenous base; a nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate; nucleic acids are long polymers of nucleotides linked by phosphodiester bonds between C3 of one sugar and C5 of the next. DNA contains 2-deoxy-D-ribose and bases A, G (purines), C, T (pyrimidines); RNA contains D-ribose and A, G, C and uracil. Watson-Crick double helix: two polynucleotide strands coil around each other in opposite directions; the sugar-phosphate backbone is outside and bases inside, paired through hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine by two H-bonds (A=T) and guanine with cytosine by three H-bonds (G≡C), so the strands are complementary. Functions: DNA stores genetic information and is responsible for replication and transfer of heredity; RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) carries out protein synthesis.
